| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

vLLM BadHost auth bypass via malformed Host header on OpenAI /v1 endpoints AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-48746 / BadHost (CVE-2026-48710) exploitation primitive: an HTTP request to a vLLM /v1/* endpoint whose Host header contains URL-structural characters (/, ?, #) that shift the reconstructed url.path so Starlette's AuthenticationMiddleware skips the /v1 auth check while FastAPI still routes the request. A legitimate Host header is only a hostname[:port], so any of these characters is high-fidelity evidence of the bypass attempt. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploitation primitive — a Host header carrying '/' or '?' (external sources add '#') against the /v1 path — which is the single most specific, low-FP signature of the bypass because RFC-valid Host headers never contain these chars. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: vLLM is a Linux Python service and none of these ship request HTTP Host headers (EDR sees only the TCP connection to port 8000). Cross-checked GitLab Advisory, OSTIF/X41 BadHost disclosure, and badhost.org. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/vllm/CVE-2026-48746/ • https://ostif.org/disclosing-the-badhost-vulnerability-in-starlette/ • https://badhost.org/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal AppSec / pentest running Burp Suite or Nuclei BadHost templates against the vLLM host
  • A broken client library that assigns a full URL (scheme://host/path) into the Host header field
  • Vulnerability scanners (Qualys, Tenable, Nessus) probing for CVE-2026-48710
  • Service-mesh / sidecar misconfiguration injecting routing info into the authority pseudo-header
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.10.20.5")   // exclude sanctioned internal AppSec scanner host(s) — replace/extend with your scanner inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the vLLM instance was started with VLLM_API_KEY/--api-key (auth enabled) and is directly exposed (not behind RFC-conforming nginx). Inspect the offending HttpHostName and HttpStatusCode — a 200 on /v1 with a poisoned host = successful bypass. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/LB, and put vLLM behind nginx or upgrade to vLLM >= 0.22.0 (Starlette >= 1.0.1) which validates the Host header. Rotate VLLM_API_KEY. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SrcIpAddr for all /v1 traffic (chat/completions, completions, embeddings, audio) to gauge model abuse/data access, and review for prompt-driven RCE attempts in request bodies.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/v1/"                                  // vLLM OpenAI-compatible API path
| where HttpHostName matches regex @"[/?#]"             // host with URL-structural chars = BadHost injection
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vLLM /v1 auth probing: 401/403 failures followed by unauthenticated success from same source AIExploitation Medium
Detects the exploitation tradecraft sequence for CVE-2026-48746: a source IP first receives 401/403 on vLLM /v1 endpoints (probing the auth requirement), then transitions to 200/201 WITHOUT supplying an Authorization header — the signature of an attacker discovering and exploiting the Host-header bypass against the same host. Rationale: Models the article's 'authentication bypass' discovery behaviour as a temporal sequence: auth-rejected probes (401/403) transitioning to unauthenticated success (200/201, no Authorization header) from the same source against the same /v1 service. The cross-status temporal join and missing-header check rule out Sigma (multi-event correlation) and Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch (no HTTP header telemetry for this Linux service). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6 • https://badhost.org/
ATT&CKT1556
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate user whose API key was initially mistyped (401) then corrected — but their success would carry an Authorization header, which this rule excludes
  • Vulnerability scanner sweeping the host then hitting an intentionally-public endpoint like /v1/models
  • Proxy briefly returning 401/403 during a config reload, then resuming with header stripped from logs
  • Load test that ramps from unauthenticated probes to traffic against an open instance
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.10.20.5")   // exclude sanctioned scanner hosts; extend with internal AppSec/LB IPs as needed
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the SrcIpAddr's request timeline — confirm the 200/201 hits genuinely lacked an Authorization header and check for a poisoned Host header on the success requests (correlate with the BadHost UC). 2) Contain: block the source IP, front vLLM with nginx or upgrade to >= 0.22.0, and rotate VLLM_API_KEY since the key gate was demonstrably bypassed. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SrcIpAddr across all endpoints and timeframes to scope data/model access, and check for any request bodies attempting downstream RCE (CVE-2026-22778 class issues) now that auth is moot.
let lookback = 7d;
let failures = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
  | where Url has "/v1/"
  | where HttpStatusCode in ("401","403")
  | summarize FailCount=count(), FirstFail=min(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName;
let successes = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
  | where Url has "/v1/"
  | where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201")
  | where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)        // succeeded with no key => bypass
  | summarize SuccessCount=count(), FirstSuccess=min(TimeGenerated), LastSuccess=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName;
failures
| join kind=inner successes on SrcIpAddr
| where FirstSuccess > FirstFail                          // probe THEN succeed
| where FailCount >= 3                                    // >=3 = deliberate probing, not a single typo
| project SrcIpAddr, ProbedHost=HttpHostName, FailCount, FirstFail, SuccessCount, FirstSuccess, LastSuccess
| order by FirstSuccess desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

New Rokarolla Android Malware Steals PINs, SMS Codes, and Crypto Wallet Funds

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 6 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Security researchers at&nbsp;Zimperium's zLabs&nbsp;have documented a new Android banking trojan, Rokarolla, that targets 217 banking and cryptocurrency apps and packs 137 remote commands. Together, they give an operator near-total control of an infected phone: it lifts lock-screen PINs, reads and sends SMS, rewrites the clipboard to redirect crypto payments, and switches off Google Play

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Rokarolla Android banker C2 beacon (beralisvc.info + .cfd fallbacks) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rokarolla Android banker C2 egress beaconing & data exfil (beralisvc.info + .cfd fallbacks) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Rokarolla Android banker C2 beacon (beralisvc.info + .cfd fallbacks) AICommand & Control High
Hunts enterprise/BYOD hosts resolving or connecting to the Rokarolla Android banking trojan's confirmed command-and-control infrastructure. Anchored on the four domains Zimperium observed in live traffic (beralisvc.info plus three .cfd fallbacks), this is a first-touch IOC match that surfaces any device that has reached Rokarolla C2. Rationale: Uses the four C2/fallback domains (beralisvc.info, blestorians.cfd, abiorime.cfd, morevoms.cfd) that Zimperium observed in live Rokarolla traffic and that Security Affairs and BleepingComputer independently reproduced — newly-registered single-purpose malware domains, so a resolution is high-fidelity. Fixed prior schema error: Sentinel now keys on DnsEvents.Computer/ClientIP, not the non-existent DeviceName column. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/rokarolla-android-banker-with-complete-device-takeover-capabilities • https://securityaffairs.com/193745/cyber-crime/new-rokarolla-android-trojan-targets-217-banking-and-crypto-apps.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-rokarolla-android-malware-targets-217-banking-crypto-apps/
ATT&CKT1437.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A corporate threat-intel/URL-detonation appliance (urlscan, VirusTotal, Joe Sandbox) resolving the domain for enrichment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst manually browsing the IOC from a managed workstation
  • A DNS sinkhole/RPZ returning a canned answer for the blocked domain (resolution logged but no real C2)
  • A different benign service that later registers one of the expired .cfd domains (domain reuse after takedown)
  • Passive DNS / recursive-resolver cache-warming traffic from a network appliance
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the device and owner; confirm whether it is a managed Android endpoint (Defender for Endpoint / MTD enrolled) or BYOD, and check the resolving process/app. Pull any Mobile Threat Defense (Zimperium zDefend) verdict for that device. 2) Contain: block all four domains at the DNS resolver/proxy/firewall, and quarantine or MDM-wipe the device; force-reset the user's banking, crypto-wallet and corporate credentials since SMS-OTP interception and PIN theft are in scope. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for the other three fallback domains, look for the sideloaded fake-TikTok/Chrome APK and a dropper posing as 'Google Play Protect', and review the user's recent banking/crypto sessions and SIM-swap/OTP activity for fraud.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("beralisvc.info","blestorians.cfd","abiorime.cfd","morevoms.cfd")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Domains=make_set(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("beralisvc.info","blestorians.cfd","abiorime.cfd","morevoms.cfd")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count(), ResolvedTo=make_set(Result) by Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by FirstSeen desc

Rokarolla Android banker C2 egress beaconing & data exfil (beralisvc.info + .cfd fallbacks) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts sustained outbound egress to Rokarolla C2 infrastructure on the proxy/firewall and EDR network layer — the channel the trojan uses to ship stolen PINs, SMS OTPs, screenshots and wallet data one frame at a time. Aggregates connection volume per host so a beaconing/exfil pattern (not just a single lookup) is surfaced. Rationale: Same four corroborated Rokarolla C2 domains, but pivots on egress connection volume (Web/proxy + EDR network) rather than first-touch DNS, catching the frame-by-frame screenshot/credential exfil and SMS-OTP relay the article describes. Fixed prior schema error: Sentinel now uses CommonSecurityLog SourceHostName/SourceIP (DeviceName is not a column on CommonSecurityLog). Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/rokarolla-android-banker-with-complete-device-takeover-capabilities • https://securityaffairs.com/193745/cyber-crime/new-rokarolla-android-trojan-targets-217-banking-and-crypto-apps.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-rokarolla-android-malware-targets-217-banking-crypto-apps/
ATT&CKT1646 T1437.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/URL-sandbox appliance repeatedly fetching the IOC for enrichment (looks like beaconing)
  • Proxy retry storms toward a sinkholed/blocked domain inflating ConnCount without real exfil
  • A monitoring/uptime probe configured against a since-reused .cfd domain
  • SOC analyst load-testing the block rule from a managed host
  • Domain takeover/parking page generating benign repeated HTTP 200s after takedown
Suppression filter
| where SourceHostName !has_any ("urlscan","sandbox","vt-","detonation")   // exclude known URL-detonation/enrichment appliances
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host, the egress volume and BytesSent, and whether the connections succeeded or were proxy-blocked; identify if it is an Android MTD-enrolled device. 2) Contain: block the four domains and any resolved IPs at proxy/firewall, isolate/MDM-quarantine the device, and reset banking + crypto-wallet + corporate credentials (assume SMS-OTP and PIN compromise). 3) Hunt: review what was sent (screenshots/SMS/wallet data), check the user's crypto transactions for clipboard-swapped attacker wallet addresses, look across the fleet for any other host touching the remaining fallback domains, and locate the dropper APK posing as Google Play Protect.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("beralisvc.info","blestorians.cfd","abiorime.cfd","morevoms.cfd")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), DistinctHours=dcount(bin(Timestamp,1h)), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Domains=make_set(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, DeviceId
| where ConnCount > 5   // repeated egress = beacon/exfil, not a one-off lookup
| order by ConnCount desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any ("beralisvc.info","blestorians.cfd","abiorime.cfd","morevoms.cfd")
   or RequestURL has_any ("beralisvc.info","blestorians.cfd","abiorime.cfd","morevoms.cfd")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), BytesSent=sum(SentBytes), Dests=make_set(DestinationHostName) by SourceHostName, SourceIP, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| where ConnCount > 5   // repeated egress = beacon/exfil, not a one-off lookup
| order by ConnCount desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("beralisvc.info")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["beralisvc.info"]);
ImNetworkSession

| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-16 11 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Unit 42 discovered a Vertex AI Python SDK vulnerability that allows remote code execution via bucket squatting. Read the article for more. The post Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vertex AI model upload to default predictable staging bucket (bucket-squat exposure) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vertex AI model deployment following default-staged upload (poisoned-model deploy) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Foreign / non-Vertex principal accessing Vertex AI staging-bucket objects · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Vertex AI model upload to default predictable staging bucket (bucket-squat exposure) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces Vertex AI ModelService.UploadModel operations that relied on the SDK's default deterministic staging bucket name ('{project}-vertex-staging-{region}') instead of an explicitly-pinned bucket. Per CVE-2026-2473, any upload using this default pattern is exposed to cross-tenant bucket squatting, so each hit must be checked to confirm the staging bucket is owned by your own project. Rationale: Anchored on the exact deterministic string '-vertex-staging-' from the article's gcs_utils.py snippet ('project + "-vertex-staging-" + location') plus the aiplatform UploadModel method; defender/sentinel/cloudwatch/falcon are empty because this telemetry only exists in GCP Cloud Audit Logs (no canonical Defender/Sentinel/AWS table). Cross-checked CVE and method behaviour against The Hacker News, CSO Online and GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-vertex-ai-sdk-flaw-let-attackers.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186193/googles-vertex-ai-sdk-could-allow-rce-through-bucket-squatting.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/google-cloud-aiplatform/CVE-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1525
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine ML pipeline uploads that intentionally use the default staging bucket already owned and pre-created in your own project
  • Data scientists running ad-hoc aiplatform.Model.upload() during model development
  • CI/CD model promotion jobs that never set staging_bucket explicitly
  • Notebook-driven experimentation where the same default bucket is reused across many uploads
Suppression filter
Refine in Datadog/Splunk by excluding uploads whose staging bucket is confirmed self-owned via a Reference Table of your project's known staging buckets, e.g. Splunk: | search NOT [ inputlookup owned_vertex_staging_buckets | fields bucket ]
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, resolve the staging bucket name '{project}-vertex-staging-{region}' and run 'gsutil ls -L -b gs://<name>' / Storage API to confirm the bucket's owning project == your project. If owned elsewhere, you are squatted. 2) Contain: halt the deployment pipeline, delete/quarantine the uploaded model version, and pin an explicit attacker-proof staging_bucket; verify google-cloud-aiplatform is upgraded to >=1.148.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate all Vertex projects/regions for the same default pattern, check whether any squatted artifacts were already deployed (DeployModel), and review GCS object-access logs on the bucket for foreign principals.

description: Detects Vertex AI model uploads that reference the SDK default deterministic staging bucket pattern '-vertex-staging-', exposed to cross-tenant bucket squatting (CVE-2026-2473).

CLOUD
index=gcp sourcetype=google:gcp:pubsub:message "data.protoPayload.methodName"="google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.UploadModel" "vertex-staging"
| rename data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail as principal, data.resource.labels.project_id as project, data.protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp as src_ip, data.protoPayload.resourceName as resource

Foreign / non-Vertex principal accessing Vertex AI staging-bucket objects AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects GCS object create/delete/get operations on objects living in a '*-vertex-staging-*' bucket performed by a principal that is NOT the Vertex AI service agent (P4SA). This catches the attacker's model-replacement write (poisoning) and model-theft reads against a Vertex staging bucket you control, the core of the Pickle-in-the-Middle race window. Rationale: Targets the 'replace the legitimate model' tamper step and model theft by filtering storage.objects.* on the article's '-vertex-staging-' bucket pattern and excluding the legitimate Vertex P4SA (gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com); GCS data-access audit is GCP-only, hence empty Defender/Sentinel/AWS/Falcon fields. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186193/googles-vertex-ai-sdk-could-allow-rce-through-bucket-squatting.html • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1530 T1565.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The user or CI service account that performed the model upload writing artifacts into its own staging bucket
  • Backup or lifecycle tooling copying/cleaning objects in the staging bucket
  • A monitoring or DLP scanner doing storage.objects.get across all buckets
  • Terraform/infra automation managing staging bucket contents
Suppression filter
Add an allowlist of expected uploader identities, e.g. Datadog: append ' -@protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail:(your-ml-pipeline-sa@*.iam.gserviceaccount.com)'
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the principal and its source IP/project; determine whether it belongs to your org's IAM and whether it should ever touch staging buckets. Note object names — saved_model.pb, *.pkl, *.joblib being overwritten is high-signal. 2) Contain: revoke the principal's access to the bucket, lock the bucket (remove public/cross-project IAM), and block deployment of any model version staged during the access window. 3) Hunt: pull all DeployModel events that referenced affected artifacts, inspect deployed model artifacts for malicious pickle __reduce__ payloads, and rotate any credentials reachable from the Vertex serving environment.

Vertex AI model deployment following default-staged upload (poisoned-model deploy) AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a Vertex AI ModelService.UploadModel that used the default '-vertex-staging-' bucket with a subsequent EndpointService.DeployModel in the same project within a short window. Deployment is the moment the staged (potentially attacker-replaced) artifact is loaded and the pickle/joblib payload executes in the serving container, so this is the last victim-visible checkpoint before RCE. Rationale: Pairs the default-staging UploadModel signal with the downstream DeployModel (the article's RCE trigger when joblib.load()/pickle.load() runs in the serving container); Sigma is empty because this is a temporal cross-event correlation, and the bare Datadog query surfaces deploys for rule-level correlation since Datadog cannot express the join inline. GCP-only telemetry, so non-GCP platform fields are empty. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-vertex-ai-sdk-flaw-let-attackers.html
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1525
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal MLOps flow where upload-then-deploy of a self-owned default-staged model is expected behaviour
  • Automated retraining pipelines that upload and immediately deploy on a schedule
  • Blue/green or canary endpoint rollouts deploying multiple model versions in quick succession
  • A/B experimentation deploying several models to the same endpoint within the window
Suppression filter
Scope the correlation to projects/SAs not on the approved MLOps allowlist, e.g. Splunk: append '| search NOT principal IN ("mlops-deployer@*.iam.gserviceaccount.com")'
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the upload's staging bucket is self-owned (see UC1); if ownership is uncertain or external, treat the deployed model as poisoned. 2) Contain: undeploy the model from the endpoint, delete the model version, and isolate/rotate any service-account credentials and secrets accessible from the Vertex serving environment (data exfil / lateral movement risk). 3) Hunt: inspect the deployed artifact for malicious pickle __reduce__ gadgets, review egress from the serving container's project, and sweep all projects for default-staged-then-deployed models on vulnerable SDK (<1.148.0).

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

Hunts the on-disk drop of SprySOCKS WIN_DRV's two encrypted kernel components — RawWNPF (KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat) and DriverLoader (KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat). These hard-coded filenames are unique to FishMonger's Windows SprySOCKS port and are not produced by any legitimate software. Rationale: Both filenames (KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat = RawWNPF rootkit, KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat = DriverLoader) are verbatim from the ESET-sourced article and are random-hash-style names no legitimate product uses, making them near-zero-FP file IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://gbhackers.com/sprysocks-windows-backdoor-uses-kernel/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html
ATT&CKT1014 T1547.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / malware analyst detonating a sample on an instrumented host
  • EDR sample-submission or quarantine copies retaining the original filename
  • Internal red-team replaying FishMonger TTPs
  • Backup/forensic image restoration re-writing a previously infected host's files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe", "MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the drop path and the InitiatingProcess that wrote the .dat — legitimate writes do not exist; pull the SHA256 and check for a co-located driver service registry key. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host from the network immediately (kernel rootkit can hide live C2); preserve memory before reboot since the loaded driver hides itself. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all endpoints for these two filenames, for kernel driver services pointing to .dat ImagePaths, and for spoolsv.exe→svchost.exe injection (WIN_PLUS sibling variant).

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat", "KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS: Print Spooler (spoolsv.exe) spawning svchost.exe injection target AIInstallation High
Hunts the WIN_PLUS execution chain where a malicious print processor running inside spoolsv.exe injects the SprySOCKS loader into a newly created svchost.exe. Legitimate svchost.exe is always launched by services.exe, never by the print spooler, so this parent→child pair is highly anomalous. Rationale: The article explicitly states WIN_PLUS uses spoolsv.exe as a print processor to inject/run a SprySOCKS loader into a newly created svchost.exe; the spoolsv→svchost parentage is a deterministic, near-zero-FP anomaly since svchost is otherwise exclusively a services.exe child. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rare third-party print driver/monitor that legitimately shells out (extremely uncommon)
  • Print management software with embedded helper that mimics svchost naming
  • EDR/AV tamper-testing harness simulating spooler abuse
  • Misconfigured legacy printing agent re-launching service host components
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-k "
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the spawned svchost command line — a legitimate svchost is launched with '-k <svcgroup>'; the doppelgänged process typically lacks a valid '-k' group. Capture the svchost child's network connections and loaded modules. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and kill the rogue svchost; stop and disable the Print Spooler service pending forensics, then dump the spool directory for the encrypted container. Step 3 (hunt): Look for a registered custom print processor (non-winprint.dll) and for the KW1B/KX1B driver .dat artifacts indicating the sibling WIN_DRV variant on the same or peer hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "spoolsv.exe"
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ChildPath = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\spoolsv.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\svchost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Custom Print Processor persistence registration (non-winprint.dll Driver) AIInstallation High
Hunts the WIN_PLUS persistence mechanism — registration of a custom Print Processor whose backing DLL is not the only legitimate processor, winprint.dll. Writes a new Driver value under the Print Processors registry hierarchy. Rationale: The article and ESET corroboration state WIN_PLUS persists by registering a custom print processor; winprint.dll is the sole legitimate processor, so any other Driver value under the Print Processors key is a high-fidelity, article-specific persistence signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html
ATT&CKT1547.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise print management suites (e.g. PaperCut, Printix) that register a custom print processor
  • Specialty label/receipt printer drivers shipping their own processor DLL
  • Printer vendor driver packages installed via printui/pnputil
  • PDF/print-to-file virtual printer software
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("printui.exe", "pnputil.exe", "msiexec.exe", "drvinst.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the DLL named in the Driver value and its on-disk path/signature — legitimate processors live under \System32\spool\prtprocs and are vendor-signed; an unsigned DLL in a temp/spool subfolder is malicious. Check the writing process. Step 2 (contain): Remove the rogue Print Processors registry subkey, delete the backing DLL, restart Spooler, and isolate the host if the DLL is unsigned/unknown. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with spoolsv.exe→svchost.exe spawns and the encrypted spool-directory container, then sweep the fleet for the same processor DLL name/hash.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Print\Environments\" and RegistryKey has "Print Processors"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Driver"
| where RegistryValueData !~ "winprint.dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Print\Environments\" and RegistryKey has "Print Processors"
| where RegistryValue =~ "Driver"
| where RegistryValueData !~ "winprint.dll"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kernel driver service installed with .dat or non-standard ImagePath AIInstallation Medium
Hunts SprySOCKS WIN_DRV kernel persistence — a driver service whose ImagePath points to a .dat container (RawWNPF/DriverLoader) or to a .sys outside the standard driver store. Legitimate kernel drivers are .sys files in System32\drivers. Rationale: WIN_DRV loads its RawWNPF rootkit via an encrypted DriverLoader, both delivered as .dat files; a kernel service ImagePath ending in .dat (or a .sys outside the standard driver store) is the registry footprint of that load and is abnormal for genuine drivers. Datadog left empty because the shipped Sysmon field set has no registry value-data attribute to filter ImagePath contents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://gbhackers.com/sprysocks-windows-backdoor-uses-kernel/
ATT&CKT1547.006 T1014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Anti-cheat / DRM kernel drivers loaded from a game install directory
  • Virtualization or security vendor drivers staged outside System32\drivers during install
  • Portable/forensic tooling loading a .sys from a USB or temp path
  • Legacy in-house hardware driver packaged with a non-standard ImagePath
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "drvinst.exe", "setup.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve the service name and ImagePath file; check the driver's digital signature and whether it is a recognized vendor — an unsigned/.dat ImagePath is malicious. Note that DriverLoader is reported as signed, so do not clear on signature alone. Step 2 (contain): Disable and delete the service key, isolate the host, and acquire memory before reboot (the loaded rootkit hides itself once running). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the KW1B/KX1B .dat filenames, the scheduled-task DLL-side-load chain, and C2 to the Vultr 207.148.64.0/20 range across the environment.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath"
| where (RegistryValueData has ".dat")
    or (RegistryValueData has ".sys"
        and RegistryValueData !has @"\System32\drivers\"
        and RegistryValueData !has @"\System32\DriverStore\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceFileName has ".dat"
    or (ServiceFileName has ".sys"
        and ServiceFileName !has @"\System32\drivers\"
        and ServiceFileName !has @"\System32\DriverStore\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SprySOCKS C2 egress to Vultr 207.148.64.0/20 (TCP/443, UDP/53, WS/80) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the WIN_PLUS hard-coded C2 infrastructure (Vultr 207.148.64.0/20), and separately flags external egress from an svchost.exe that was spawned by spoolsv.exe — the injected backdoor's network channel over TCP, UDP and WebSocket. Rationale: The C2 range 207.148.64.0/20 (Vultr; TCP:443/UDP:53/WS:80) is reported in second-source coverage of the WIN_PLUS samples, and the svchost-parented-by-spoolsv egress clause ties network activity back to the article's specific injection chain — both are far narrower than generic beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate services hosted elsewhere in Vultr's 207.148.64.0/20 (shared cloud range)
  • Corporate VPN or SaaS app that happens to use a Vultr-hosted endpoint
  • Security/uptime scanners probing the range
  • svchost legitimately reaching a public IP for Windows Update/telemetry (filtered by the spoolsv-parent clause)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the local process making the connection and whether the remote IP is reached by other hosts; a Vultr IP contacted by a single endpoint via svchost spawned from spoolsv is a strong true positive. Confirm protocol mix (443/53/80). Step 2 (contain): Block 207.148.64.0/20 at the perimeter, isolate the host, and snapshot memory (kernel rootkit may mask the connection on-host). Step 3 (hunt): Pull the host's process tree for the WIN_PLUS injection chain and the print-processor persistence, and search DNS/proxy logs for other hosts beaconing to the same range.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "207.148.64.0/20")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
        and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "spoolsv.exe"
        and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "207.148.64.0/20")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposure hunt: unpatched CVE-2023-24932 Boot Manager (BlackLotus/UEFI bootkit risk) AIExploitation Low
Surfaces hosts still exposed to CVE-2023-24932, the Windows Boot Manager security-feature bypass that ESET cites as a possible UEFI bootkit vector in some SprySOCKS intrusions. This is an exposure/hunting query to prioritise patching of the revocation mitigation, not a behavioural alert. Rationale: CVE-2023-24932 is the only CVE named in the article (the Boot Manager bypass behind BlackLotus, patched by Microsoft in May 2023); enumerating still-exposed hosts via the TVM table is the actionable defensive pivot for the article's UEFI-bootkit hint. Cross-checked against: • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1014
Data sources
Expected false positives — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts reporting the CVE but where the boot revocations were applied manually (TVM lag)
  • Recently reimaged machines pending the next TVM scan
  • Dual-boot/Linux machines flagged by OS inventory noise
  • Devices where the staged revocation rollout is intentionally deferred per Microsoft's phased guidance
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the device truly lacks the CVE-2023-24932 revocation mitigation (the fix is a staged Secure Boot DBX/boot-policy update, not a single KB) and cross-check against any SprySOCKS endpoint findings. Step 2 (contain): For any host that also shows SprySOCKS driver/print-processor artifacts, treat as potential bootkit compromise — isolate and plan offline reimage/firmware validation rather than in-place cleanup. Step 3 (hunt): Apply the revocation update to exposed hosts and review boot integrity (Measured Boot/TPM logs) on high-value targets in the affected geographies (Honduras, Taiwan, Thailand, Pakistan).
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2023-24932"
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId == "CVE-2023-24932"
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceName
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

| eval delta = _time - prev_time

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-06-16 15 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Since late 2025, malware has been spreading rapidly through the Steam Workshop, the gaming platform's built-in service for players to create and share custom content. The attackers are primarily targeting gamers in China and Russia.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Steam wallpaper campaign payload hash sweep (DarkKomet / Lumma / Vidar / RenEngine)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Wallpaper Engine spawning LOLBins or staged binaries (Steam Workshop wallpaper malware) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Campaign loader '._cache_GAME1.exe' execution (Steam wallpaper malware) · [LLM] DarkKomet Synaptics.exe backdoor executing from ProgramData · [LLM] DarkKomet 'Synaptics Pointing Device Driver' Run-key persistence to ProgramData · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 communication to Steam wallpaper campaign infrastructure (120.48.156.17 / 202.144.192.29) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Tampered AggregatorHost.dll loaded/dropped (Steam session credential theft) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Wallpaper Engine spawning LOLBins or staged binaries (Steam Workshop wallpaper malware) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Wallpaper Engine host processes (wallpaper32.exe/wallpaper64.exe) spawning script interpreters, rundll32/regsvr32, the campaign loader/backdoor, or any child executing from Temp/AppData/ProgramData. Application-type wallpapers run arbitrary code, so a wallpaper process parenting a shell or an unsigned drop is the core execution signal of this campaign. Rationale: Anchors on Wallpaper Engine's documented host binaries as parent plus the campaign's named loader (._cache_), DarkKomet drop (Synaptics.exe), and user-writable execution paths. The parent+child pairing keeps it tighter than a bare LOLBin hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/steam-workshop-abused/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate application-type wallpaper (CPU/GPU widget, mini-game) that genuinely launches a helper exe from AppData
  • Wallpaper Engine auto-updater extracting and running an installer from %Temp%
  • Power-user wallpaper authors testing scenes that shell out to cmd/powershell
  • Steam overlay or anti-cheat helper spawned under the wallpaper process tree
Suppression filter
| where not(FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-update","installer") and FolderPath has @"\Steam\steamapps\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256; check whether the parent wallpaper was installed via Steam Workshop in the last few days and whether the child is signed. 2) Contain: if the child is unsigned/from Temp or matches Synaptics.exe/._cache_, isolate the host and kill the process tree; quarantine the wallpaper package directory. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for AggregatorHost.dll loads, Synaptics.exe persistence, and outbound traffic to 120.48.156.17 / 202.144.192.29.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","Synaptics.exe")
    or FileName startswith "._cache_"
    or FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\wallpaper32.exe", @"\wallpaper64.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\rundll32.exe", @"\regsvr32.exe", @"\mshta.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\Synaptics.exe", @"\._cache_", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Wallpaper Engine Spawning LOLBin or Staged Binary
id: 6f3c1d8a-2b41-4e9c-9a7d-7c2e1f0a4b55
description: Wallpaper Engine host process spawning a script interpreter, LOLBin, the campaign loader/backdoor, or a binary from a user-writable directory, consistent with malicious Steam Workshop application wallpapers.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wallpaper32.exe'
      - '\wallpaper64.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\Synaptics.exe'
  selection_path:
    Image|contains:
      - '\._cache_'
      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\Roaming\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
  condition: selection_parent and (selection_child or selection_path)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\wallpaper32.exe OR *\\Wallpaper32.exe OR *\\wallpaper64.exe OR *\\Wallpaper64.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\Synaptics.exe OR *\\._cache_* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/wallpaper(32|64)\.exe/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|rundll32|regsvr32|mshta|wscript|cscript|Synaptics|_cache_)/i OR ImageFileName=/\\(Temp|AppData|ProgramData)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
